summary: An informational memo from the Internet architecture community that makes two recommendations to improve Internet performance: test and widely deploy active queue management in routers, and keep working on better end-to-end congestion control. It was replaced by RFC 7567.

eli5.summary: When too many cars arrive at a toll booth, a smart booth starts warning drivers early instead of waiting for a huge traffic jam. This memo urges routers to do that.

questions: how to avoid internet congestion in routers
what is red random early detection
why do routers drop packets before the queue is full
subtitle: A 1998 memo urging routers to drop packets early, before queues fill, and calling for work on flows that ignore congestion.

tldr.problem: Routers that drop packets only when a queue is full let queues stay full, lock out some flows and cause bursts of losses, while flows that ignore congestion signals threaten the network.
tldr.mechanism: The memo recommends active queue management in routers, with Random Early Detection (RED) as the default for FIFO queues, and urges research into handling unresponsive or more aggressive flows.
tldr.outcome: This Informational memo has been obsoleted by RFC 7567 and updated by RFC 7141.

facts.label: Drop probability range
facts.value: 0 to maxp, linear between the thresholds

today: RFC 2309 is an Informational memo that has been obsoleted by RFC 7567 and updated by RFC 7141, so read those for the current guidance.

sections.title: Why Routers Need Help With Congestion
sections.content:
The Internet's connectionless design is flexible and robust, but it needs careful design to give good service under heavy load. Without it, the network can suffer "Internet meltdown", technically called congestion collapse, first seen in the mid 1980s. Van Jacobson's congestion avoidance mechanisms, which began in 1986 and are required in TCP implementations, make TCP flows responsive: they back off when the network drops packets.

The memo argues those mechanisms are necessary and powerful but not sufficient, because there is a limit to how much control can be exercised from the edges. Routers need mechanisms too. It separates queue management, which controls queue length by dropping packets, from scheduling, which decides which packet is sent next and shares bandwidth among flows. The discussion covers best-effort traffic.
sections.eli5: Drivers who slow down when it is crowded help a lot, but the road itself needs help too. The memo asks the road, meaning the routers, to do its part.

sections.title: The Problem With Tail Drop
sections.content:
The traditional method sets a maximum queue length and drops new arrivals once it is reached. This is tail drop, and it has two drawbacks. Lock-out lets one connection or a few flows monopolize the queue and keep others out. Full queues arise because tail drop signals congestion only when the queue is already full, so queues stay full or nearly full for long periods.

Full queues hurt because packets arrive in bursts. If the queue is nearly full, a burst causes several drops, which can make many flows throttle back together (global synchronization) and then leave the link underused. The memo's counter-intuitive point is that normally-small queues can give both higher throughput and lower delay. Queue limits should reflect the size of bursts to absorb, not the steady state.

Random drop on full and drop front on full fix lock-out but not full queues. The fix for responsive flows is to drop packets before the queue is full, which the memo calls active queue management. Its stated benefits are fewer dropped packets, lower delay for interactive traffic and no lock-out. It does not claim better fairness, since general fairness needs per-flow state, and it says queue management and scheduling are complementary.
sections.eli5: If a waiting room is always packed, a sudden crowd has nowhere to stand. Keeping it fairly empty leaves space for surprises and keeps the wait short.

sections.title: Random Early Detection
sections.content:
RED drops arriving packets probabilistically, and the chance of a drop grows as the estimated average queue size grows. It reacts to a time-averaged queue length, not an instantaneous one, so a queue that was mostly empty recently will not drop packets, while one that has been fairly full will.

It has two parts. First, it estimates the average queue size with an exponentially weighted moving average, with a special case when a packet arrives at an empty queue. Second, it decides whether to drop using two thresholds: minth, below which no packets are dropped, and maxth, above which all are dropped. Between them the drop probability rises linearly from 0 to maxp. The decision can be made in packet mode or byte mode.

The memo says the available evidence shows substantial benefits and seemingly no disadvantages, and that RED should be widely deployed. It admits an extreme case where RED will not cure the problem: a very large number of flows, each so small that its fair share is less than one packet per round-trip time.
sections.eli5: The booth does not wait until the line is out the door. The longer the line has been lately, the more likely it is to ask a newcomer to come back later, and that makes people slow down in time.

sections.title: Aggressive and Unresponsive Flows
sections.content:
Sharing a congested link fairly works because flows run basically the same congestion avoidance algorithm. The memo defines a TCP-compatible flow as one that responds to congestion notification and uses no more bandwidth in steady state than a conformant TCP under comparable conditions. It then names two threats.

  • Non-responsive flows, such as UDP streaming applications like packet voice and video and multicast bulk transport, that do not slow down. The memo says all UDP-based streaming applications should include effective congestion avoidance, and that the network also needs ways to protect itself.
  • Non-TCP-compatible transports that respond to congestion but take an unfair share, through poor implementation or on purpose. Opening multiple connections to the same place, as some Web browsers do, is a known way to be more aggressive without changing TCP.

Identifying and isolating such flows at acceptable cost is hard, and the RFC says there is little measurement evidence about how fast the threats will grow. It also notes that the right granularity of a flow, such as a connection, a host pair or a single host, is partly a policy question for the wider IETF.
sections.eli5: A road works when everyone slows down in traffic. A few drivers who never slow down, or who sneak extra cars in, can spoil it for everybody.

sections.title: The Two Recommendations
sections.content:
Recommendation 1: Internet routers should implement some active queue management mechanism to manage queue lengths, reduce end-to-end latency, reduce packet dropping and avoid lock-out. For FIFO queues the default is RED, unless a developer has reasons to provide another equivalent mechanism.

Recommendation 2: It is urgent to begin or continue research, engineering and measurement on mechanisms for flows that are unresponsive to congestion notification or are responsive but more aggressive than TCP. The memo stresses that deploying RED alone would not achieve this second goal.

It adds that wide RED deployment would enable other functions, such as explicit congestion notification as an addition to packet drops, and queues with different drop priorities. On security, it says the topic is largely separate from performance, but denial-of-service attacks can create unresponsive flows that look like normal high-bandwidth traffic, so the mechanism of Recommendation 2 would apply to them as well.
sections.eli5: Two requests: let every router start nudging drivers early, and keep studying how to handle the drivers who never listen.

items.title: 1. Active queue management
items.text: Routers should drop packets early to keep queues short. RED is the default for FIFO queues.

items.title: 2. Handle aggressive flows
items.text: Research and measure ways to manage flows that ignore congestion or are more aggressive than TCP.
